common_name: White Gloria Astilbe (Weisse Gloria, Classic White Arendsii Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, organically rich soil in partial shade; a classic Arendsii white cultivar, distinct from the similarly white Bridal Veil astilbe in bloom timing and plume density.

directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1-2 inches below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade. White Gloria bears dense, feathery plumes of pure white flowers in midsummer above glossy, deeply cut dark green foliage, giving a shaded border a cooling, bright accent among the pinks and reds of most other astilbe cultivars. Astilbe does not tolerate drought, so mulch well and water consistently, especially through a hot Gulf South summer, and it appreciates a bit more morning sun than most shade perennials as long as soil moisture stays high. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom, and leave the dried flower plumes standing into winter for continued texture in the garden.

common_name: Hyacinth Astilbe (Classic Deep Pink-Lilac Arendsii Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, organically rich soil in partial shade; an old German Arendsii cultivar still grown for its rich, deep pink-lilac plumes.

directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1-2 inches below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Hyacinth bears dense, upright plumes in a rich, deep pink-lilac shade, opening in early to midsummer above finely divided, dark green foliage on one of the older, longer-established Arendsii hybrid astilbe cultivars still commonly found in nursery trade. Its strong stems and dense plume make it useful for cutting as well as garden display. Astilbe does not tolerate drought, so mulch well and water consistently, especially through a hot Gulf South summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.

directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1-2 inches below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Aphrodite emerges with bronze-tinted young foliage that matures to dark green, providing a rich backdrop for its dense, dark salmon-pink flower plumes in mid to late summer, a deeper and warmer color than many pastel pink astilbe cultivars. Its compact size fits well toward the front of a shaded border or in a mixed container planting. Astilbe does not tolerate drought, so mulch well and water consistently, especially through a hot Gulf South summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Younique Silvery Pink Astilbe (Compact Early-Blooming Heavy Shade Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, organically rich soil in shade; a sibling in the Dutch-bred Younique series noted for tolerating heavier shade than most astilbe cultivars.

directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1-2 inches below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in shade. Younique Silvery Pink produces soft, silvery-pink plumes on a compact plant bred, like its sibling Younique Salmon, to tolerate deeper shade and to bloom earlier than standard astilbe cultivars, making it useful for the darker corners of a woodland bed where other flowering perennials struggle. Spent flower heads dry to an attractive tan color that provides continued texture into winter if left standing. Astilbe does not tolerate drought, so mulch well and water consistently, especially through a hot Gulf South summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Little Vision in Pink Astilbe (Dwarf Compact Pink Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, organically rich soil in partial shade; a dwarf sport of the popular Visions series bred for edging and container use.

directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1-2 inches below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Little Vision in Pink is a dwarf selection from the popular Visions line of Astilbe chinensis hybrids, producing the same dense, upright raspberry-pink plumes on a noticeably smaller, more compact plant well suited to edging a shaded path, tucking into a rock garden, or filling a mixed container where full-sized astilbe would overwhelm the space. Astilbe chinensis types tolerate somewhat drier soil than Arendsii hybrids, though consistent moisture still produces the fullest bloom. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigor and bloom quality.

common_name: Hennie Graafland Astilbe (Compact Pale Pink Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, organically rich soil in partial shade; a compact, floriferous Dutch-bred Arendsii cultivar useful for smaller shaded borders.

directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1-2 inches below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Hennie Graafland produces abundant, dense plumes of soft pale pink flowers on a compact, well-branched plant that blooms heavily relative to its smaller size, making it a good choice for the front of a shaded border, edging a path, or filling a mixed container. Its manageable footprint fits into smaller garden spaces better than taller astilbe cultivars while still delivering a strong summer flower display. Astilbe does not tolerate drought, so mulch well and water consistently, especially through a hot Gulf South summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Glow Astilbe (Glut, Deep Carmine-Red Arendsii Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist, organically rich soil in partial shade; an older German Arendsii cultivar prized for one of the deepest red-carmine plume colors in the class.

directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1-2 inches below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade. Glow, also sold under its German name Glut meaning "ember," bears dense, upright plumes in a deep carmine-red that glows against its dark green, bronze-tinted foliage, one of the richest red tones available among Arendsii astilbe hybrids. It blooms in midsummer and combines well with the cooler pinks and whites of companion astilbe cultivars for a layered color display in a shaded border. Astilbe does not tolerate drought, so mulch well and water consistently, especially through a hot Gulf South summer. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Superba Chinese Astilbe (Tall Lavender-Pink Species-Type Astilbe)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring or early fall in consistently moist soil in partial shade to full sun; Superba is noticeably more drought- and heat-tolerant than most Arendsii hybrid astilbe cultivars, a trait inherited from its Chinese species parentage.

directions: Plant crowns so the top of the rhizome sits 1-2 inches below the soil surface in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade, though it tolerates more sun than most astilbe as long as soil moisture is adequate. Superba sends up tall, narrow, bottlebrush-like plumes of lavender-pink flowers on stiff upright stems well above the foliage, blooming later in the summer than most Arendsii hybrids and standing considerably taller, which makes it useful toward the back of a shaded border or massed as a late-summer color accent. Its Chinese species parentage gives it noticeably better tolerance of heat and brief dry spells than typical astilbe cultivars, though it still performs best with consistent moisture. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to maintain vigorous bloom, and leave the dried seed plumes standing for winter interest.
